idiom_name: Future/ExecutionContext for the async layer with a dedicated blocking ExecutionContext
implementation_notes: Scala puts the asynchronous layer in the Future/ExecutionContext model: computations are scheduled on an ExecutionContext whose global implementation is a ForkJoinPool sized to the available processors, and continuations run without blocking. The synchronous layer is deliberately a separate ExecutionContext - the docs recommend wrapping long-lasting blocking operations in their own context or Java Executor, and Akka/Pekko name the same idea a blocking dispatcher - while the queueing layer is an explicit bounded java.util.concurrent queue or an actor/stream mailbox. Keep the layered split where blocking libraries (JDBC, legacy HTTP clients) cannot be made non-blocking.
pitfalls: Blocking inside ExecutionContext.global - a JDBC call, Await.result, a semaphore - starves the ForkJoinPool and can deadlock unrelated futures; a dedicated blocking context (or the blocking construct) is required.
Await.result inside another future pins a thread and destroys the layering; use map/flatMap/onComplete or a callback-based bridge.
A blocking ExecutionContext is still a pool: an unbounded queue in front of it hides overload instead of signalling it.
